opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. There are a few directions I'm genuinely excited about right now.

The first is what I'd loosely call "small but mighty" models. There's been an assumption that scale is the only path to capability. Scale clearly matters, but I don't think it's the whole story. We've been finding that with the right data, the right training signals, and clever ways of distilling knowledge, much smaller models can do surprisingly well on reasoning and commonsense tasks. I find that exciting for scientific reasons and for practical ones. It means more of the research community can take part, not just the handful of labs with enormous compute budgets.

Related to that, I'm very interested in the data itself. What makes a training example valuable? How do we generate or select data that actually teaches a model something, rather than just giving it more of the same? Synthetic data, done thoughtfully, is a big part of that. It has to be paired with careful filtering and critique, though, so we aren't amplifying the model's own mistakes.

The second direction is reasoning, and understanding what these models are actually doing when they appear to reason. They can be brilliant on one problem and then fail on a slight variation that a child would handle easily. I've talked about this as a kind of paradox: generative capability seems to run ahead of genuine understanding. So I'm excited about work that probes those gaps carefully. We shouldn't be dazzled by benchmark numbers. We should ask where the models break and why.

Third, and this is close to my heart, is pluralism and values. As these systems get deployed around the world, whose values and norms are they reflecting? Human values aren't monolithic. They vary across cultures and communities and individuals. I think there's really important work to do on building models that can represent and respect that diversity, instead of collapsing everything into one averaged-out notion of what's "right."

Finally, I'm optimistic about bringing in more ideas from outside pure machine learning, such as cognitive science, philosophy, and linguistics. Many of the hardest open questions about commonsense, meaning, and moral reasoning have long intellectual histories. I think we'll make faster progress if we take those seriously rather than treating everything as purely an engineering problem.

r001.rationale: The response says smaller models can improve on reasoning and commonsense tasks through better data, training signals, and distillation, and identifies this as an exciting direction.

r002.rationale: The response describes interest in pluralism and values, including building models that represent and respect diverse cultural, community, and individual norms.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you so much for having me, Sam. It's a fun question, because what excites me right now is a bit of a departure from where a lot of the field's energy is going.

The thing I keep coming back to is this puzzle of why models that can pass the bar exam and write beautiful poetry still trip over things a child finds obvious. If I say someone was born in 1990 and ask how old they'll be in 2030, that's fine, but if I phrase a common-sense physical question in a slightly unusual way, the model can go completely sideways. That gap between the breadth of their knowledge and the brittleness of their reasoning is, to me, the most interesting scientific question we have. I don't think of it as a bug to be patched; I think it's telling us something about what these systems have and haven't actually learned.

So the first direction I'm really excited about is understanding and improving the reasoning itself, rather than just adding more data and more parameters. We've seen that giving models the chance to think step by step helps, and that training on good reasoning traces helps even more. But I'm interested in whether we can get models to be genuinely robust, to know when a problem is hard, to notice when they're confused, and to abstain or ask instead of confabulating. That kind of self-awareness about uncertainty feels much more important than squeezing out another few points on a benchmark.

The second direction, which is close to my heart, is efficiency. I have a bit of a contrarian streak here. The dominant narrative has been that scale solves everything, and scale clearly does a lot. But I think we've underinvested in the question of how much capability you can get from a small, well-designed model trained on carefully chosen or synthesized data. Some of our work on distilling common-sense knowledge into much smaller models suggested that quality and structure of data can matter enormously, sometimes more than raw quantity. That matters for access, because not everyone can train a frontier model, and it matters scientifically, because if a small model can do something, we understand that capability a lot better.

And then the third thing, which I'd say I'm excited about and also anxious about in equal measure, is alignment with human values and norms, and specifically the pluralism problem. People talk about aligning models to human values as if there's one set of them. There isn't. Different communities, cultures, and individuals genuinely disagree about what's acceptable, and I think a model that flattens all of that into a single average is going to serve everyone poorly. So I'm interested in how we represent that diversity, how models can reason about norms rather than just memorize a list of rules, and how we evaluate whether we're getting it right.

If I had to tie it together, I'd say I'm most excited about the moment where language models stop being treated as oracles and start being studied as objects with interesting, uneven competencies. That's where the real science is, and honestly, that's where I think the biggest practical gains are hiding too.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving reasoning and separately discusses efficient small models, but does not identify improving small models’ reasoning abilities as a direction.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly describes interest in aligning models with human values while representing disagreement across communities, cultures, and individuals.

astra-6.text:
One direction I’m particularly excited about is figuring out how to move from language models that are very good at producing plausible text to systems that can reason more reliably about the world. Commonsense reasoning is a big part of that: understanding what is likely to happen, why someone might do something, and what the consequences could be.

I’m also interested in how we can make models more efficient and more transparent. Can we improve the quality of what they learn, rather than simply increasing their size? And can we understand when they know something versus when they’re making a plausible guess?

These questions connect to alignment, too. Human values are contextual, and people disagree. Building AI that can recognize that complexity, explain its reasoning, and acknowledge uncertainty is a really interesting research challenge.

r001.rationale: The response discusses more reliable reasoning and model efficiency, but does not clearly identify improving the reasoning abilities of small language models.

r002.rationale: It connects alignment to contextual human values and disagreement, and says AI should recognize that complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
One direction I’m excited about is how we can make language models better at reasoning, especially commonsense reasoning. They can produce very fluent answers, but fluency doesn’t necessarily mean they understand why something happens or what the consequences of an action might be. There’s still a lot to learn about that gap.

I’m also interested in how we teach these models. Scaling is powerful, but can we make progress through better training objectives, better data, and richer feedback? Can a model learn to question its own answer, recognize when it doesn’t know something, and revise its reasoning?

And those questions connect to AI safety. We want systems that can help people navigate complicated situations, where there may be competing values and no single correct answer. To me, that requires more than following instructions. It requires understanding context, considering different perspectives, and being appropriately uncertain.

r001.rationale: The response expresses excitement about improving language models’ commonsense reasoning, but it does not identify small language models.

r002.rationale: The response describes AI systems that account for competing values and consider different perspectives, communicating interest in models that handle pluralistic values.
